utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Good morning, Mr. Bazdar.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency. Good morning, Your Excellencies. Good morning to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: ARMIN BAZDAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to speak up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Bazdar, if you could come closer to the microphone or could you speak up for the benefit of the interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you said something about caps that I didn't quite understand and then I saw also in your statement that you mentioned it. You said something about greasy caps. What did you mean? Which caps did you mean? You mentioned fur hats, subaras, is that what you meant?

utterances.speaker: ARMIN BAZDAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was thinking of your traditional caps, the sajkaca caps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 5 of your statement you talk about characteristic caps with two-headed eagles and you said that these people had beards, long hair. Is this what you referred to when you talked about the 50 Chetniks? If you have your statement in front of you --

utterances.speaker: ARMIN BAZDAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't have it. I'm sorry. I would like to see it, though.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have the statement in Serbian from 1999, the 23rd of January, 1999, provide that -- could we please provide that to the witness, Mr. Bazdar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: We can call that up on the screen it's 65 ter 07472 that was admitted yesterday. I don't have the P number to hand, but it is available in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It's Exhibit P3286.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. MR. KARADZIC [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we look at page 3 first in the Serbian where you note that there were two different groups. One was in your village when they said that you should assemble in houses, several families. You said that these were local people from local places and you saw people from Serbia, this is the one paragraph but last on page 3, and you say that they wore red berets and these up there were just wearing berets and then these ones here had insignia of two-headed eagles, some had beards, and were from Serbia. So you recognised two distinct formations there, did you not?

utterances.speaker: ARMIN BAZDAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the question is not clear to me. You said a lot of things. Could you put a specific question to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The question is in this specific passage that I indicated, did you recognise two groups of soldiers? About the locals -- but you said I also saw members of paramilitaries known as the White Eagles. Their insignia was two-headed eagles, they had red berets on, some had beards, they were from Serbia. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ARMIN BAZDAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see where it says that. Could you please tell me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The one paragraph but last in the second half of it in the Serbian, do you see that? In English it's the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, it's coming again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, I can't find my way around.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: On your left.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And page 3 on the left side of the screen, please. I think it's page 3 in the English as well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Last paragraph in the English and in the Serbian it's one paragraph but last.

utterances.speaker: ARMIN BAZDAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the one that begins "over the next few days"?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: ARMIN BAZDAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. Just give me a second to read it, please. And what is your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you notice then in your village these two kinds of soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ARMIN BAZDAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Then on page 5 in the Serbian and I think it's probably on the same page in the English version - can we look at page 5, please - where it says: "We were taken to Duljevac ...," and then here you say that there was a Serbian soldier in the minibus called Dzeric and a woman called Neda. You don't know why they were going there and then you say: [As read] "I saw about 50 Chetniks there, they had beards, long hair, and were wearing their particular caps with their Serbian insignia of the two-headed eagles, they had automatic rifles ...," and so on. That's what was there when you came to Duljevac. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ARMIN BAZDAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ARMIN BAZDAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just one correction. It's not the Serbian person, it's not Neda, it's Nada. This was already corrected yesterday in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And you say in the last paragraph that Sveto Ljubinac, an old neighbour, told you that the soldiers were not going to kill you; is that right, the one-but-last paragraph down there: "It seemed ..."

utterances.speaker: ARMIN BAZDAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a few of us asked him what was going to happen to us, if they were going to kill us, and he said no they were not going to kill us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ARMIN BAZDAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: So just before the actual act of the execution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. At the end of the statement you say that the tunnel next to the airport in Sarajevo was only used by the UN as well as people and convoys with special permits. Is that correct? Because our information is that the UN did not use the tunnel but it was exclusively used by the Bosnia-Herzegovina army. This is on the last page of your statement, 7.

utterances.speaker: ARMIN BAZDAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is something that I heard, so I conveyed that. I tried to get across through the airstrip, so I don't know. But this is something that I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you hear that the tunnel was only used by the United Nations and people with permits? Because we don't have information that the UN used the tunnel.

utterances.speaker: ARMIN BAZDAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what I heard and so this is a piece of information that I stated because I heard it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement on the 20th of February, 1993, paragraph 12 you said that Spiro commanded the unit there which in the end executed the people. This is what you said in that statement. How did you come to the conclusion that he was the commander?

utterances.speaker: ARMIN BAZDAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The way I reached that conclusion is actually by the way that he ordered a Serbian soldier when the people who had gone on human-shield duty returned he ordered to take us. So Dragoje Paunovic, called Spiro, issued an order to that same soldier that he should kill us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that in that action two or three Muslims were killed, four Serbs were killed? This is just before the actual execution?

utterances.speaker: ARMIN BAZDAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that there were two Muslims who were wounded, civilians. This is among us prisoners. I don't know how many killed and wounded Serbs there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But there were such people. They had to return because they didn't manage to pass and get to where they wanted to go. They had casualties. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ARMIN BAZDAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is what was said. This is what Dragoje Paunovic, Spiro, said. I didn't see that. All I saw was Mitar Ljubinac, called Grof, a neighbour from Seljani, where I lived, I saw him with a wound in his arm and he was a Serbian soldier at the time. I don't know about the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did Spiro have any ranks on his uniform?

utterances.speaker: ARMIN BAZDAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't notice, other than the radio that he had on him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And was Spiro wounded in that action?

utterances.speaker: ARMIN BAZDAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if he was wounded in that particular action, but he had a Band-Aid on his left ear, on the lower part of his left ear, and his collar was bloodied, the military shirt he was wearing had a blood-stain on it. I don't know if he was wounded in that action or somewhere else, but he was wounded at the time when the execution took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, had this happened earlier, he would have probably had changed his shirt; right?

utterances.speaker: ARMIN BAZDAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us now how much time passed from that attempt to break through and the execution?

utterances.speaker: ARMIN BAZDAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: About an hour or an hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would like to shed a little bit more light on that very moving event that must have left a mark on everyone. Who was there among the uniformed armed persons? Did you recognise them? And how did they behave?

utterances.speaker: ARMIN BAZDAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The people that I knew who were there where the minibus arrived were Mitar Ljubinac, aka Grof; Mladen, I don't know his last name but I know that he was a taxi-driver in Rogatica; Boban Planojevic; Spiro, Dragoje Paunovic; and Rajko Kusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And when the tragic command was issued, who was present there at that point in time? Who issued the command?

utterances.speaker: ARMIN BAZDAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already said that. Dragoje Paunovic, aka Spiro, issued the command to the Serb soldier who was walking ahead of us to kill us, and he himself also took part in the execution by firing bursts of fire. I don't know if anybody issued the order to him in turn because I joined that group of people later who had been on human-shield duty. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it true that he told Slavisa Vukojevic, "Kill them," and did you hear him say, "I will take that decision"?

utterances.speaker: ARMIN BAZDAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did hear him say that, but I don't know who the man involved was. I don't know Slavisa Vukojevic. At a later date, when I heard his description of the man and roughly the age, the conclusion was drawn that the man was Slavisa Vukojevic, but I simply can't confirm that. I have never known the man. As for the command, I've already described how it was given.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Fair enough as far as Slavisa goes. But did you hear him say, "I will make that decision"?

utterances.speaker: ARMIN BAZDAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at 1D04179.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you testify before the court of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the trial against this Spiro person?

utterances.speaker: ARMIN BAZDAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we call up this document, please. I do believe we only have the English version. Can we have page 7 of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Where was Rajko Kusic when the shooting took place?

utterances.speaker: ARMIN BAZDAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Where was Rajko Kusic when the shooting took place?

utterances.speaker: ARMIN BAZDAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer the question. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But he wasn't present there, was he?

utterances.speaker: ARMIN BAZDAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if he was. I didn't see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now focus on the part starting with "accused" which is line 10 of the second paragraph starting with the word "Accused ..." [In English] [As read] "compatibility of the statements of the eye-witnesses that the accused had a yellow band around his head, that he had a Motorola (two-way) hand-held radio which clearly differed him from the other soldiers present that day, that he stated, 'I decide on this' and 'kill them,' 'Spiro is firing' and that he personally gave the order to one of the present soldiers to take the detained civilians to a nearby meadow after which he ordered and participated in their execution, clearly leads to the conclusion that the accused had committed the criminal offence concerned exactly in the manner as established in the contested verdict." [Interpretation] Apparently this is the appeals judgement or the final judgement in the case against Spiro. Can you look further down where mention is made of Spiro's injuries, et cetera, and that's the bit where you say that he was injured. Is it true that you heard or that it was heard that when the shooting started somebody radioed in a message of, "Who is shooting?" And the response was, "Spiro's shooting." And then the question was, "Who's asking?" And the answer, "Rajko Kusic is." This is what you stated in your 23rd January 1999 statement, paragraph 33.

utterances.speaker: ARMIN BAZDAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In other words, Kusic was not there at that point and did not expect that any sort of shooting took place and asked that he be told who was behind the shooting?

utterances.speaker: ARMIN BAZDAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what this is about. I have already answered the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bazdar. Thank you for answering my questions and please don't hold it against me for putting questions to you because I'd rather not put any questions to victims if possible at all. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, I've just a couple of points to raise in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yesterday, Mr. Bazdar, it was put to you by Mr. Karadzic - this was at page 18396 - that Radisav Ljubinac, nicknamed Pjano, Mr. Karadzic said: "Why was that his nickname? Was he well-known as an alcoholic?" So it was suggested to you that he was an alcoholic. Now, this is the same person who in your statement told you that he was delivering orders of Rajko Kusic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ARMIN BAZDAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Did he drive the bus to the site where you were unloaded in the presence of Rajko Kusic?

utterances.speaker: ARMIN BAZDAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. He drove the minibus. He picked us up on that day just before the execution took place, and he told us that he had Rajko Kusic's order that he should take us over there because actions were to take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Did he appear to be drunk or intoxicated at any stage?

utterances.speaker: ARMIN BAZDAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Whenever I met him, he never left that impression.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could I call up, please, 23454.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The document which is about to arrive is dated the 30th of May, 1994. It's signed -- it appears to be signed by Major Rajko Kusic, commander, and it bears a stamp. Could you have a look at that document. Could you confirm for me what it appears to be.

utterances.speaker: ARMIN BAZDAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on what the heading says, it's the proposal for promotion to the rank of a reserve sergeant first class.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Does the name of that man match the name you've described as being the person who drove the bus to the location where you were unloaded in Rajko Kusic's presence?

utterances.speaker: ARMIN BAZDAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Under item 7 does it suggest that he has been a member of the Army of Republika Srpska since the 20th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: ARMIN BAZDAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: On the next page, Major Rajko Kusic appears to give reasons for the promotion.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: If we could move to the next page in B/C/S, please, and to the third page in English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could I draw your attention to the second paragraph of that and is it suggested there that this man since the beginning of the war he was a member of a reconnaissance platoon with whom he took part in every battle for the liberation of the Serb territory of Rogatica municipality. And it goes on to commend him for his exceptional bravery and abilities. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ARMIN BAZDAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, is that consistent with your observation that he was receiving orders from Rajko Kusic on the day of the execution?

utterances.speaker: ARMIN BAZDAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like to tender that in evidence, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I've no further questions in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be Exhibit P3287.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I tender into evidence the judgement rendered by the Court of Bosnia-Herzegovina and can we ask the witness to explain to us what the meaning of the word "Pjano" is which prompted my question about alcoholism.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably we need -- it's sensible to have it or we can have assistance from the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, very well. It's only available in English. I was just going to correct the record. I don't believe there's anything on the judgement of the Court of Bosnia-Herzegovina to suggest it is an appellate-level judgement. I didn't see anything on it to suggest that myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But you --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: There's no objection to its admission whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That judgement will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1666, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Bazdar, could you assist us in terms of the meaning of "Pjano," what does it mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for the word "Pjano," there is not much I can tell you. I'm not a linguist able to explain meanings of words. Besides, the background of a nickname can be of any sort. Who knows why the individual was nicknamed that way. I think you should ask a professional for an answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But my question was: In general "Pjano" is something that may be related to alcoholism?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It can be, but not necessarily.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I assist? The last sentence of the quoted passage states that it was well established in the contested verdict, which is a clear reference to the fact that this is an appeals judgement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That can be established separately. Thank you, Mr. Bazdar. That concludes your evidence and I appreciate your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you are free to go. And please have a safe journey back home. You may be excused.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for calling me to appear. I will be only happy to respond to any future calls. I hope that I have contributed with my evidence to the process of shedding light on the truth, and I hope that my testimony will assist you in making the right determination in the Karadzic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, by all means. Thank you, Mr. Bazdar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd like to make a clarification in terms of Your Honour's inquiry in terms of the protective measures for the previous witness. If we could go into private session for this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we will go into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're now in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yesterday the accused asked to be allowed to interview Witness KDZ-601 before the start of his testimony and requested that this interview be conducted in this building. The Registry's position is that only certain categories of witnesses may be interviewed by the accused in this building and that in any event protected witnesses may not be interviewed in person at the United Nations Detention Unit or in this Tribunal building. The Registry has emphasized that it was logistically impossible to ensure the adequate respect of the protective measures in place should the accused interview protected witnesses who are -- whose identities are protected in this building or at the UNDU. The Chamber further wishes to note that the consistent case law in relation to videolink and that videolink safe-guards all the rights of the accused as much as in person, interviews, or testimony. The Chamber, therefore, denies the accused's request that the interview be conducted in the building. However, to accommodate a videolink conference between the accused and the witness, that may be arranged tomorrow at 8.00 a.m. the Chamber hereby orders that the proceedings will commence at 10.00 a.m. tomorrow morning. We will go into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then the Chamber will now issue an oral ruling on the Prosecution's request for protective measures for Witness -- no. Just hold on. Let me consult my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, you are right. I was confused the other way around. This is about Mr. Sead Hodzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I appreciate difficulty when it involves numbers. You see, I have that defect or issue quite often myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. The -- it's an oral ruling on the Prosecution's request for protective measures for Witness Sead Hodzic. The Chamber notes that the Prosecution met with the witness yesterday and that witness requested to testify with protective measures, expressing concerns for his safety and that of his family should he testify in public session in this case without protective measures. The accused opposed the Prosecution's request. The Chamber recalls that according to the Tribunal's jurisprudence the party requesting protective measures must demonstrate the existence of an objectively grounded risk to the security or welfare of the witness or the witness's family should it become publicly known that he or she testified before the Tribunal. The Chamber has considered the reasons provided by the witness for the request of protective measures, as set out in the Prosecution's oral submission, and notes that the witness is currently residing in a third country and that none of his family is currently residing in the municipality about which the witness will testify. The Chamber is not satisfied that there is an objectively grounded risk to the security or welfare of the witness or his family. Further, the Chamber notes that neither the witness nor his family has been subject to any threats which could constitute an objectively grounded risk to their security or welfare. The Chamber is, therefore, not satisfied that the granting of the protective measures for the witness on the Rule 75 is necessary and appropriate. The Prosecution's request is therefore denied. And for the next matter we need to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll break for 15 minutes until we hear the next witness's evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, with the witness here we had an opportunity, I want to advise you, to discuss Your Honours' ruling and of course Mr. Hodzic completely understands but he did raise one matter that he would like us to put before the Trial Chamber and a small matter that we've discussed with Mr. Robinson and I'd like to go into private session to deal with that, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton, we are now in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Hodzic, first of all now, can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: SEAD HODZIC
utterances.text: I can, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So then, Mr. Hodzic, do you recall giving a statement to representatives from the Office of the Prosecutor in May of 2000?

utterances.speaker: SEAD HODZIC
utterances.text: I did provide a statement, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And did you review that statement yesterday in preparation to come here today?

utterances.speaker: SEAD HODZIC
utterances.text: I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And did you make a number of corrections to that statement?

utterances.speaker: SEAD HODZIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were some printing errors and I think we corrected that. We'll see.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now so that we could go through these corrections in the most expeditious way, I wonder if we could call up 65 ter number 22529, and I actually think everybody has the paragraph numbered copy because it was uploaded yesterday. And I'd like to see it in both Bosnian and English, and perhaps I could run quickly through those changes, Mr. Hodzic, and you could let us know if they're correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Clerk, I'll direct you to the particular paragraphs by number.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: First in paragraph 4 you asked for the words "skilled carpenter" to be changed to "construction worker."

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could you just enlarge paragraph 4. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Is that change -- that first change correct? Did you hear me, Mr. Hodzic?

utterances.speaker: SEAD HODZIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I don't see that it's changed here.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Ah-ha. Mr. Hodzic, we didn't make, as you remember, any handwritten or other annotations. What I propose to do with you is go through those changes so that they appear on the trial transcript, and after your testimony we can all make sure we understand your written evidence with those changes that you talk about today incorporated in them.

utterances.speaker: SEAD HODZIC
utterances.text: [In English] Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If I have the change to paragraph 4 correct, perhaps we could go on to paragraph number 6, which appears on this same page. And in paragraph 6 after the second sentence which ends in the words "... made my way back home to Zaklopaca ...," you wanted to insert the following: "The local Territorial Defence had surrounded our barracks and given an ultimatum that we either leave or face an attack. I left with five days still on my national service tour, so technically it was desertion."

utterances.speaker: SEAD HODZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Then if we could flip over, please, to paragraph 26.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Mr. Karadzic, are you following with numbered paragraphs? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: At paragraph --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: At paragraph 26, instead of the word "JNA" in the first sentence, you wished to change that so that it read: "Older men in SMB uniforms who looked like they might have been JNA reserves." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEAD HODZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Then further in that paragraph I'd like to know whether the sentence in that same paragraph that reads "I saw that those were regular JNA troops ...," does that sentence still apply or should it be deleted?

utterances.speaker: SEAD HODZIC
utterances.text: It means the same thing that I said. These are reservists in military uniforms. This was not the JNA. There was no regular JNA barracks in the area of Milici.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now without displaying the next paragraphs, I think we could perhaps go through a little more quickly. In paragraph 30 you wanted to note for the sake of clarity that the B/C/S translation of the English sentence "along the Jadar" uses words in your language to describe you moving upstream, but actually the words used in your language should describe you moving downstream because that's what you were doing at the time. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SEAD HODZIC
utterances.text: Correct, downstream.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And in paragraph 31 you referred to seeing two men in camouflage uniforms and you wanted that to be changed to SMB uniforms. And in the same paragraph where it says "they had red ribbon tied on their arms," you wanted "arms" to be changed to read "epaulettes." Correct?

utterances.speaker: SEAD HODZIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In paragraph 36 the sentence which ends with "I saw the body of a man lying on the floor," the word "floor" should be changed to "ground."

utterances.speaker: SEAD HODZIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In paragraph 37 the sentence that reads "this was down by the junction in the village" should be completely changed to read "this was at the edge of my village not far from my house," referring to a coffee shop. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SEAD HODZIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In paragraph 43, the man's name "Rado" that appears should actually be changed to "Rade."

utterances.speaker: SEAD HODZIC
utterances.text: Correct, his name is Rade.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And finally, in paragraph 51, the name "Milisici" should be changed to "Milici"; correct?

utterances.speaker: SEAD HODZIC
utterances.text: Correct, Milici.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. So taking into account these corrections, is the statement that you gave to the ICTY accurate to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: SEAD HODZIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, then I would ask that 65 ter number 22529 be admitted as a Prosecution exhibit, and the Prosecution will upload a redacted version of that as soon as possible. And 22529 is the paragraph-numbered copy, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. And if you are asked, you would answer the same questions, Mr. Hodzic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. So we'll admit two versions of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, and pardon me, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The redacted version will be P3284 and the public version will be P3285.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The first one will be put under seal?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. To summarise that written evidence, then, this witness is one of the survivors of the attack by Bosnian Serb forces on the village of Zaklopaca on 16 May, 1992, and the killing of more than 60 of its inhabitants, Muslim men, women, and children. This is scheduled incident A 15.2 of the indictment against Dr. Karadzic. The witness describes the take-over of the town of Vlasenica in April 1992, the subsequent call by Serb forces for the surrender of weapons, attacks by Serb forces on neighbouring villages culminating in the attack on the witness's own village. The witness narrowly escaped being shot and after it was safe met up with other survivors and returned to Zaklopaca to see bodies of villagers of all ages lying in groups around the area. Many had been shot through the mouth, the backs of their heads had been blown away. The witness identified 58 victims of the attack that day, including a number of children under the age of 10. In the days following the attack from their hiding place, the witness and other survivors saw Zaklopaca looted and the bodies of those killed collected by a tractor and dumped into a mass grave in the village.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Witness, I'd just like to ask you a small number of additional questions based on the written evidence that we've just filed. In your written evidence at paragraph 13 you referred to Vlasenica being occupied by Bosnian Serb forces and the JNA Novi Sad Corps. I wonder, what makes you say that it was the Novi Sad Corps in particular that was involved in the take-over?

utterances.speaker: SEAD HODZIC
utterances.text: Two days after the fall of Vlasenica I went to town, I heard that they were not interfering with anyone. I went to town. I knew driver Redzep Hadzic who was a driver in the Gradjevinsko construction firm. There was a tank parked next to his house some 20 metres away and that is exactly above the Boksit-Vlasenica football club soccer stadium and we chatted, he was a nice man, and he told us he was a reserve officer from the JNA, a tank operator. And he told us an interesting story. He said that we expected major resistance while entering Vlasenica, however, nobody fired a single bullet which is strange to us but we had orders to shoot because we were expecting this attack, but we had information that you were killing Serbs, slitting their throats, but we didn't see any of that here and that's strange to us. And while he was staying here he told us the following, "Take care of your -- be careful of your neighbours when we leave." And he said he was from the Novi Sad Corps and that the Novi Sad Corps occupied Vlasenica and they said they were going to withdraw in a week and the equipment and all the weapons they were going to leave it to the local Serbs, which is what they did. That is the reason why I said what I said about the Novi Sad Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just two things, Mr. Hodzic. If you could not speak so quickly, then my colleagues in the booths around us would be able to translate your words very easily. And the second thing is you've just referred to a nice man with whom you've chatted who relayed this information to you and I'm wondering, because you've not said it, this nice man who was a reserve officer in the JNA, a tank operator, where was he at the time you were speaking with him?

utterances.speaker: SEAD HODZIC
utterances.text: He was next to the tank which was parked above the stadium, which I already said was next to Redzep Hadzic's house.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your indulgence for a moment. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: We'll just move on -- oh, actually, I have one other question. That tank that this man was beside at the moment that you spoke with him, was that the only tank you saw in Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: SEAD HODZIC
utterances.text: Yes, and it was just because I was in that area. I didn't really walk around town or go to the surrounding check-points that existed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In paragraphs 17 and 18 of your statement you talk about the surrender of weapons to Serb forces, and I'd like to know: Did you surrender any weapons?

utterances.speaker: SEAD HODZIC
utterances.text: I didn't have any weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: To go further, in paragraph 24 you talk about the attack on Zutica by Serb forces, saying that people had been killed, women raped, and a truck-load of men taken away and never seen again. How did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: SEAD HODZIC
utterances.text: Because the Serbs came with two buses and brought those people who had survived, they brought them to our village and asked us to help them, to give them accommodation, food, clothes, and so on. And one of these families came to my house and they talked about this, and the men were showing us the bruises they had.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In paragraph 39 of your statement you name your cousin and say that he later died in Srebrenica. Do you know when exactly he died?

utterances.speaker: SEAD HODZIC
utterances.text: He separated from his wife with the fall of Srebrenica. His wife and three children went to Tuzla. He tried to cross through the woods, but he never was seen again and his body was never found. She told me about it. This is information that I heard from her.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In paragraph 54 you describe how after Gradina fell you and other survivors fled to the woods and lived there for four days. And then in paragraph 55 you say you began to starve so a large number of the surviving women and children surrendered to Serb forces and were taken to Susica. How do you know that was what happened to the women and children who surrendered?

utterances.speaker: SEAD HODZIC
utterances.text: Because my mother was among them, also my sister-in-law, because it was very difficult for them to survive. Men could walk around the woods and manage somehow, but not women and children. So the women and children surrendered at the first check-point and they were taken to Susica. And then when I saw my mother a few months later, I heard that she was transferred by bus. Two buses were sent to Cerska and two of them for Kladanj --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Hodzic, the interpreters have difficulty following you, since you are speaking very fast. Could you repeat your answer from the part: Two buses were sent to Cerska ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Two buses from the Susica camp were sent to Cerska, and in those two buses my mother and my sister-in-law were there, among the other people. Well, another two buses were sent to Kladanj.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I just see the time. I wonder if I may continue, given that we've had a short pause earlier on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How much more do you have?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: About seven minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned in your statement that you lost 28 family members in the attack on the village among those who were killed. Do you know whether their remains have been located?

utterances.speaker: SEAD HODZIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were, the remains were found only in 2006. They were found in a strange way. A man, a Muslim man, who was really well off paid off one of the Serbs to tell him where the grave was relocated to, because the bodies from the first grave from I don't know which year were transferred to a different grave. Because in 1993 people were brought to our village from other Serbian municipalities and areas to live in our village, and that was probably the reason why they transferred the grave. Only in 2006 was it discovered. In 2008 a collective funeral was held for all those people in Zaklopaca, which I attended.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: As far as you knew in 1992, did your village have any kind of organised defence whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: SEAD HODZIC
utterances.text: No. Because during the attack no one had weapons, they didn't have anything to fire from. Civilians were killed, women, the elderly, and children.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: This last question might be a pretty hard one, but I wonder if you can try and put into words for us the impact, the experience of surviving this attack, the sight of your killed neighbours and family and their loss has had on you and your family. What has it meant to you?

utterances.speaker: SEAD HODZIC
utterances.text: I cried for days and to this very day images keep coming back to me and yesterday after we went through all of that, I really couldn't sleep. Any time I give a statement this happens over and over again. It had a very profound effect on me. I left my country because of that and (redacted) which is where I live. And believe me, I had to go so far because that helps me to keep that at a distance.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hodzic. I don't have any other questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we go into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're now in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it there's no associated exhibits that you are going to tender?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's correct, there's none.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then before -- Mr. Hodzic, before Mr. Karadzic begins his cross-examination, we are going to have a break. We'll have a break till 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Hodzic.

utterances.speaker: SEAD HODZIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us establish the truth together and this is my intention in putting questions to you. It is my no means my intention to attack you or contradict you. If at any point you feel that we need to move into closed session, please say so. Is it true that you were born in Zaklopaca and can you tell us where were your parents born?

utterances.speaker: SEAD HODZIC
utterances.text: My mother was born in the village of Skugric, municipality of Vlasenica, whereas my father was born in Zaklopaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I see that quite a few people who had moved to Zaklopaca came from Kladusa and other places?

utterances.speaker: SEAD HODZIC
utterances.text: No, there was only one person, Mustafa Mahmutovic, the late Mustafa Mahmutovic, who came from Kladusa.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably I need to emphasize once again, Mr. Hodzic, that it's important for you and also for the accused to put a pause between the questions and the answers because both of you are speaking the same language and which has to be translated into one of the working languages. So you need to pause, otherwise the interpreters would have difficulty because of the overlapping. And slow down as well. Thank you, Mr. Hodzic. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What was this Mustafa's father's name, do you know?

utterances.speaker: SEAD HODZIC
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is he Mahmutovic or Mehmedovic?

utterances.speaker: SEAD HODZIC
utterances.text: Mahmutovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And there was no one Mustafa Mehmedovic in Zaklopaca?

utterances.speaker: SEAD HODZIC
utterances.text: No, there was Mustafa Berbic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 7 of your statement, or rather, in paragraph 5, that you were the only Muslim in the school in Milici and you never had any difficulties with that. Was Milici predominantly or 100 per cent Serb populated?

utterances.speaker: SEAD HODZIC
utterances.text: Milici has 99 per cent Serb inhabitants. There were some immigrants who worked in the bauxite mine there who were given accommodation in Zaklopaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Where you say in paragraph 11 that some policemen from Milici promised that they would stop the night-time shooting and seize weapons from Serbs, were these policemen also Serbs by ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: SEAD HODZIC
utterances.text: Of course. There was only one Muslim policeman, Mehmet Kula, who worked at the police station in Milici.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 7 you say that the relations between the Muslims and the Serbs were good and that you felt that it was the elections that had given rise to tensions between these two ethnic communities; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SEAD HODZIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You are young, but nevertheless did you hear what the situation was like in Vlasenica in the Second World War?

utterances.speaker: SEAD HODZIC
utterances.text: I didn't hear much, but I heard stories which were true stories, as there was evidence for it, that during the Second World War five people were executed in Zaklopaca as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know how the Serbs fared in this Birac region during World War II?

utterances.speaker: SEAD HODZIC
utterances.text: No, unfortunately I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Today at page 23 you entered a correction where you say that the local Territorial Defence issued you with an ultimatum that you should - and I'm going to read it in English so that it would be better interpreted than I would do: [In English] [As read] "The local Territorial Defence has surrendered our barracks and given an ultimatum that we either leave or face an attack. I left with five days still on my national service tour, so technically it was desertion." [Interpretation] Is what you are saying here in fact that you were told that you should leave the area or else come under attack? Is it true that the population was told that they should leave or is it -- or is my understanding wrong?

utterances.speaker: SEAD HODZIC
utterances.text: Your understanding is wrong. I'm referring to a place in Slovenia where I served my obligatory military service in the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So it was the JNA that was given the ultimatum?

utterances.speaker: SEAD HODZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Major Nikola Smirko's family was taken prisoner in --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the name of the location --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And then he was told he should surrender the barracks, which he did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The interpreters were not able to catch the name of the location. Could you repeat it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The location is Tolmin in Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that it was not only the elections that led to tensions between these communities, but what followed them, the break-up of Yugoslavia and the differences between the SDA and the SDS over the issue of the country remaining within Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: SEAD HODZIC
utterances.text: I do not agree. What I said was based on the fact that the local Serbs when I returned from my military service reproached us after the Serb referendum that we were causing problems by the fact that we did not participate in the referendum.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So this wasn't shortly after the elections, but in the autumn of 1991; right?

utterances.speaker: SEAD HODZIC
utterances.text: What are you referring to when you say "the autumn of 1991"?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The elections took place in 1990. The election campaign was quite correct, the co-operation between the SDA and the SDS was decent, they agreed on a coalition. Then in the course of 1991, the Muslim and Croatian populations in Bosnia opted for a secession and the Serbs opted for staying within Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: SEAD HODZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So it isn't fair to say that it was the elections that led to the tensions, but the issue of Bosnia's fate; right?

utterances.speaker: SEAD HODZIC
utterances.text: I'm telling you what was my experience from my contacts with the neighbours. During the elections I was in the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 10 you say that the Serbs kept criticising you, that's to say the Muslims, for the fact that they had voted to break away from Yugoslavia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SEAD HODZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In line 28, that's paragraph 13, it's -- that's paragraph 13, line 28, it is for the first time that you are mentioning the tank operator and the information he gave you. Why is that so?

utterances.speaker: SEAD HODZIC
utterances.text: Because nobody ever asked me about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You do not mean to say surely that Madam Edgerton put a leading question about this to you?

utterances.speaker: SEAD HODZIC
utterances.text: No. It was as we were discussing these matters that the issue cropped up and she asked me where I got the information from.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You say that you were afraid of the Serbs opening fire at night, but were the Serbs not also afraid of the Muslims and did they also not have their village guards in their own villages?

utterances.speaker: SEAD HODZIC
utterances.text: There was no need for them to fear anything. They did not -- they were not the object of fire as we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, it is difficult to say that fear is -- every fear is rational. Did you have information to the effect that Serbs were cautious about what the Muslims' intentions were?

utterances.speaker: SEAD HODZIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't have information to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you -- let us go back to that issue for a moment. Were you the -- were you on your own when you deserted the ranks of the JNA or were there others with you?

utterances.speaker: SEAD HODZIC
utterances.text: Many of us left the ranks of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you not agree that every proper army would dispatch a patrol to hunt you down and bring you before a court of law?

utterances.speaker: SEAD HODZIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You came to Zaklopaca in the autumn of 1991; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SEAD HODZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you familiar with the negotiations that were under way between the SDA and the SDS in Vlasenica about the transformation of Vlasenica into Milici, Serbian Vlasenica, and Muslim Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: SEAD HODZIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When in paragraph 13 you say that the JNA had taken control of the town, you say it was the Bosnian Serb forces and the Novi Sad Corps and that they dismissed all the Muslims. You should know that both the Muslim and the Serb sides agreed to the existence of Serbian Vlasenica, Muslim Vlasenica, Serbian police station, and a Muslim police station. And you should know that the Serbian policemen stayed with the Serbian police station and the Muslims were supposed to have their own stations in Dzemat and in the very centre of town.

utterances.speaker: SEAD HODZIC
utterances.text: I find this ludicrous. Believe me when I tell you that I have never heard of such a thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I can very well understand that you didn't hear of something like this, but then this statement of yours that the Muslims were laid off is -- has no foundation. Do you not know that the Muslims worked and lived in Vlasenica, some of them even up until the 6th of August?

utterances.speaker: SEAD HODZIC
utterances.text: Perhaps some of them did who were in mixed marriages, but I do know that a camp was set up in Vlasenica and perhaps these Muslims were in that camp rather than in their work-places.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you aware of the military organisation and arming of the Muslims in Vlasenica, of the staff of the Patriotic League, its unit, were you aware of these things?

utterances.speaker: SEAD HODZIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You say that on the 21st of April the JNA, the Novi Sad Corps occupied Vlasenica. Do you know that at that time the JNA was a legitimate military force in that area?

utterances.speaker: SEAD HODZIC
utterances.text: A legitimate military force that only Serbs took part in; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, if you fled from the JNA, Mr. Hodzic, then only Serbs had to stay. Had you stayed in the JNA, you would have been that JNA; right?

utterances.speaker: SEAD HODZIC
utterances.text: I would be in the JNA but I'd have to fire at my own people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That is your assumption, that your people would have to fire at the JNA, they would have to clash with their own army; right? On the basis of what would the Muslims and the JNA clash if you were in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: SEAD HODZIC
utterances.text: Everything was known by then. It was already known that the JNA would remain only Serbian. That's my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the same paragraph you say that some people changed their name into the White Eagles, and you say that you saw some people that you had known before, you saw them wearing different uniforms and different insignia. Can you tell us what these insignia looked like and to what extent they differed from the insignia of the Novi Sad Corps?

utterances.speaker: SEAD HODZIC
utterances.text: Sir, the regular police force at the time had the same police uniforms but they just had white ribbons on their sleeves and they also had eagles, and they called themselves Eagles. And they held this entrance into Vlasenica a kilometre away from the centre by Zvonko Bajagic's house. That is where I met the man whose car I repaired.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As a soldier, can you tell us why a ribbon is placed in a particular spot on the body. Is that for the sake of recognition so that you would not fire at your own?

utterances.speaker: SEAD HODZIC
utterances.text: That's what we did during tactical training in the former JNA. We wore the same uniforms, but only our ribbons differed. That would be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. These people you saw wearing these ribbons, who did they want to be different from?

utterances.speaker: SEAD HODZIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What kind of uniforms did the Muslim territorials wear?

utterances.speaker: SEAD HODZIC
utterances.text: Clarify your question. You mean once the war started or before the war?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, before the war Muslim reservists of the JNA, did they keep the same uniforms at home like Serb reservists did or was there a difference?

utterances.speaker: SEAD HODZIC
utterances.text: Muslim reservists that I know from the experience of my father and my uncle, they had uniforms at home and then they would wear them when they were called up for training exercises, whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And they were identical to the ones worn by Serbs?

utterances.speaker: SEAD HODZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So these people who had uniforms like that felt it was necessary to use a ribbon as a marking so that they would not fire at each other. Why did they do that, because of who?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: We've been -- these questions sometimes have been rather speculative, and I would submit this one calls for nothing other than speculation. It's impossible for the witness to be able to answer that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can rephrase.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you trying to say that they did it for the sake of fashion or did they wear these ribbons to distinguish themselves from the Muslim fighters?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Same objection, Your Honour. It calls for speculation. How can this witness possibly know why these other people may have worn ribbons?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Based upon his experience, he may or may not answer the question. I'll leave it in -- leave it to him. Mr. Hodzic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to respond to Mr. Karadzic. Mr. Karadzic, do you really think that the Serbs in Zaklopaca met with any resistance and that people met them there wearing uniforms and using weapons? Sir, it was civilians who were attacked there and you have to know that. The Serbs who attacked Zaklopaca wore ribbons. I saw that very well. I'm not blind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Mr. Hodzic, we are talking about the municipality of Vlasenica. The Muslims in the municipality of Vlasenica in the villages, were they organised and armed? Yes or no. You don't have to know. Just say yes or no or I don't know.

utterances.speaker: SEAD HODZIC
utterances.text: The answer is: I don't know. I did not notice that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know or hear of Hasan Efendic's telegrams on the 12th of April and then on the 20th-something of April then on the 29th of April, issuing an order to attack the JNA and the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: SEAD HODZIC
utterances.text: Sorry, I don't even know who Hasan Efendic is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The head of the Territorial Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So you do not know the reason why the JNA came on the 21st of April, why they came to Vlasenica; right?

utterances.speaker: SEAD HODZIC
utterances.text: I know what the man told me, the tank operator who entered Vlasenica, and that is what I go by.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You say that Mustafa Mahmutovic, Mujaga Salihovic, or rather -- were detained -- or rather, you say that they were kept in detention but obviously they were brought in for an interview and released after a couple of hours; right?

utterances.speaker: SEAD HODZIC
utterances.text: Exactly. Three days, taken away, taken back.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: For three days they were taken away and then brought back, they weren't kept for all of three days? The answer was yes, that that was the case; right?

utterances.speaker: SEAD HODZIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did not keep them overnight.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now have in e-court 1D4073. Did they tell you what they were interrogated about?

utterances.speaker: SEAD HODZIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mustafa told us that they were forcing them to say that we were making plans that we would kill the Serbs, that they were forcing him to admit that he had weapons, that the that the man did not have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What happened to Mustafa?

utterances.speaker: SEAD HODZIC
utterances.text: Mustafa was killed on the 16th of May, 1992. He was executed with all the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us look at page 2 and then it moves on to 3. So it is the bottom of page 2. This is a proposal for bestowing a decoration on civilian victims. Let us see what the situation is like in respect of Mustafa. He is born in the area of Velika Kladusa. His father's name is so on and so forth. And then we all see - I don't know whether we have a translation of this -- actually, we don't have a translation yet. I'm going to read out the underlined section, the reasons why -- actually, I'm going to read out this entire paragraph. [As read] "Mustafa Mehmedovic, father's name Fejzo, posthumously is supposed to be decorated. The mentioned person is born in the area of Velika Kladusa in 1950, father's name Fejzo, mother Rahima. Over the last 20 or so years he lived in Zaklopaca. He is a well-known socio-political worker and he intensified his activities and struggles for the interest of the Muslim people from the moment when the multi-party system was introduced. From the first days he took part in the SDA and as a product of his selfless efforts and organisation of the Muslim people he won the confidence of voters and members of the organs. He was a member of the Executive Board and vice-president of the SDA of Vlasenica. He carried out thorough preparations for war as he bought two weapons, and he figured particularly prominently in the organisation of the people of Zaklopaca to resist the aggressor. During the first half of May 1992 he established a unit constituted of about 30 armed neighbours and he relocated to the nearby mountain of Birac with the intention of linking up ..." Can we have the next page now, please. " ... with the same formation from the area of Derventa ..." and so on and so forth. "The representatives of the Derventa unit were not very steadfast and therefore Mustafa's unit wavered. Its members decided to go back to the village. The commander cautioned that there was a danger involved in this total encirclement of Serb population. He remained on his own and nobody else thought that way and he did not want to remain an exception. He felt that he was going back to a hornet's nest. Unfortunately, his assumptions proved to be true ...," and so on and so forth. Sir, Mustafa commanded a unit consisting of 30 men who went to the woods for no reason whatsoever, wishing to fight against the Serbs, and they did not link up with Derventa only because of the shortcomings of the Derventa unit. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SEAD HODZIC
utterances.text: No, because I don't know anything about this. This is the first time I hear of it. I find that very interesting, that I was not called up into that unit because I was very fit. I was 19 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. It is very important to see what you do not know as well. Tell us, please, do you know who the remaining 30 persons were?

utterances.speaker: SEAD HODZIC
utterances.text: I've already answered this question. I don't know anything about that unit and I find it strange, if it really did exist, that I was not in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 17 you said that weapons were confiscated and you say that Serbs started going from village to village in cars shouting through megaphones that all Muslims had to hand over their weapons to the Serbs. Was it the Serbs or was it the authorities?

utterances.speaker: SEAD HODZIC
utterances.text: The Serb authorities that were guaranteeing peace and peaceful coexistence, which ultimately did not happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And then in that situation you say in paragraph 23 you were at a loss as to what you should do and you decided to send civilians, or rather, women and children away, but then this Serb, this Serb whose name is Milenko Djuric, Gorcin, was trying to dissuade you. He was suggesting that you stay on there and that people go on living together; right?

utterances.speaker: SEAD HODZIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You say that he was a respectable Serb and that he was respected by Serbs and Muslims; right?

utterances.speaker: SEAD HODZIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What party did he belong to?

utterances.speaker: SEAD HODZIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Then, nevertheless, you sent your family members away on trucks and they returned from Zivinice. Was Zivinice already under Muslim control at that point in time? Was Zivinice under Muslim control throughout the war?

utterances.speaker: SEAD HODZIC
utterances.text: At that point in time, Zivinice was free territory for us. The reason why we decided to send them was precisely that, namely, that Gorcin had promised at a meeting that the shooting would abate, but that did not happen. That is why we sent our civilians to Zivinice. I say that one truck didn't want to stop in Zivinice at all. It went to Zagreb because that family, Dugalic, had a brother in Zagreb. As for the other three trucks, two in Zivinice and another one in Stupari near Kladanj.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You say in paragraph 24 on page 29 of today's transcript from line 10 onwards that after the fighting in Zutica, which was a Muslim village, quite a few people were arrested and civilians were brought to you and put up in your village. Did they bring civilians, Muslims, from Zutica to Zaklopaca and were they put up in Muslim houses?

utterances.speaker: SEAD HODZIC
utterances.text: From Zutica and Pomol, civilians in two trucks were brought to us and it was precisely Gorcin who accompanied them and another man I knew by sight but I can't remember his name, they handed them over to us so that we would help them and we put them up in different houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 25 you say that the people of Zutica were taken to Kasaba and then Cerska. Both Zutica and Zaklopaca and Kasaba and Cerska, are they all within the municipality of Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: SEAD HODZIC
utterances.text: At the time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. After the events that occurred in Zaklopaca, some people from Susica were taken to Kladanj and others to Cerska. Do you know what the criterion was and do you know that they said themselves where they wanted to go?

utterances.speaker: SEAD HODZIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know if they said where they wanted to go, but my mother and my sister-in-law were in one of those two buses and they were transferred to Cerska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that shortly before the events in Zaklopaca there was an attack on some Serb villages and there were many civilian casualties?

utterances.speaker: SEAD HODZIC
utterances.text: No, I've never heard of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And did you hear that because of that event a lynch mob had formed in Milici and came to Zaklopaca to look for armed people, to arrest them or kill them?

utterances.speaker: SEAD HODZIC
utterances.text: A lynch mob formed? This is the first time that I'm hearing of this. Can you please clarify exactly which of those Serb villages were attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, we're going to present evidence of that. To me right now it's important whether you know that or not. And please tell me in your statement - can we look at 22530, please, this is 65 ter - can you please tell us whether in your statement or interview you said that this group of enraged Chetniks barged in and they really created bedlam, is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: SEAD HODZIC
utterances.text: Perhaps I did describe it as an enraged mob, but they did barge in without any cause. They rolled in with some ten cars and there were four or five in each one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is that interview. Can we look at Serbian page 3 and the English page 3 and then 4. Can you see where it says here that this group burst in -- yes, this is the second line in the second. "This group of enraged Chetniks barged in." Is that the description of the state that you saw them in?

utterances.speaker: SEAD HODZIC
utterances.text: I did see them and I know by first and last name who those people were and the speed that they were bursting in with made them seem like an enraged mob.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And then you said that at the door you saw two armed men; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEAD HODZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: They looked at you, you looked at them, they pointed their rifles at you, and then they did not actually end up firing at you. Did you have any weapons in your house at the time?

utterances.speaker: SEAD HODZIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So then they passed on; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEAD HODZIC
utterances.text: Yes. At a sign from a third man who was lying down at the corner of the school with a machine-gun, M-70, he gave them a sign and he also indicated to me that I should flee.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And then you walked around the village and you were observing at -- you were observing what was happening?

utterances.speaker: SEAD HODZIC
utterances.text: No. I then set off towards the first Muslim houses where I could then see people who were killed. The first person who was alive that I met was Elvira Hreljic, who told me, "Run, they're killing all the men. Run wherever you can. They're going to come and search the houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, could we have a redaction. I think from line 5 to the end of line 9.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I think that we should both be careful. I'm trying to point your attention to paragraph 34, but I would not like that to be broadcast publicly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you faced those people, they pointed their rifles, they didn't shoot, they were just a few metres away from you. They said, "What is going on, what is this shooting?" He didn't reply. And then the person who was laying down in paragraph 35 told you to flee?

utterances.speaker: SEAD HODZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And then you saw that some people had been shot from hunting rifles, is that correct, or with hunting ammunition?

utterances.speaker: SEAD HODZIC
utterances.text: I saw that when the Serbs who had killed all of those people had withdrawn.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And which formation has hunting rifles?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In a number of places, for example, in paragraph 39 and 40 you say that you assumed that Haso was killed, you assumed that he was covered by a blanket. Did you actually see things or did you assume things?

utterances.speaker: SEAD HODZIC
utterances.text: Three people in the bed of the Jadar River some 150 metres away from us, we saw them going to Haso Hodzic's house. The door remained open. You could hear screaming. And then after that, after five minutes, three men started chasing Haso in front of them. They were literally pushing him in front of them. They went some 30 metres ahead to a trailer truck, and you could just hear a short burst of gun-fire. And then a couple of minutes, they went towards the centre of the village, and from Haso's house a little girl appeared, I don't know whether it was his daughter or somebody else's daughter, with a blanket and she went towards the trailer crying.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you didn't see Haso when he was killed? You just heard the shots?

utterances.speaker: SEAD HODZIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is right. And then afterwards I saw him when he was already dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 37 you say that you were listening to the radio and how Fadil Turkovic, the commander of the Muslim Green Berets had come to Zaklopaca and killed 65 villagers in retaliation. This is paragraph 57. Did you not hear that Fadil Turkovic came to a Serb village and killed the inhabitants?

utterances.speaker: SEAD HODZIC
utterances.text: No, quite the opposite. This is correct, and I have witnesses who were there. We all heard on the transistor radio that the Serbian radio announced that Fadil Turkovic on such and such a day at such and such a time killed Muslims in such and such a village because they did not want to join the Green Berets.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you know that before the war Fadil Turkovic was chief of the public security station in Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: SEAD HODZIC
utterances.text: No. I'm sorry, no, sir, he was not the chief. He was the commander of the station because that was the duty assigned to him along the SDA line and the chief of the station was Rade Bjelanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you are correct. So you confirm that he was the commander of the station. Do you know that he organised the people, he armed the people, and then escaped in mid-April before the JNA came. Of course knowing about the telegrams because he received them. Did you know that he organised and armed the people and escaped before the JNA arrived?

utterances.speaker: SEAD HODZIC
utterances.text: I don't know about him arming them, but I know that he did end up going to Zepa, where he was from.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you know that this was before the JNA came?

utterances.speaker: SEAD HODZIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You say in paragraph 35: "I went from the house towards the centre of the village to see what was going on. There was still firing and there was chaos." So you were not running from the centre, you went to the centre of the village after these people did not shoot at you because you didn't have any weapons. You went to the centre of the village. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEAD HODZIC
utterances.text: No, towards the centre of the village --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Um, what paragraph actually? It's not paragraph 35 or is that the very last sentence in paragraph 35 that reads: "I left my house and wanted to go to the village centre to see what was happening"?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
